name: Pale Neropalin Blue
lede: Pale Neropalin Blue is a soft greyish blue, the pale tone Robert Ridgway charted beside the parent color Neropalin Blue in his 1912 color atlas.

sections.title: A pale tone of Neropalin Blue
sections.body:
Pale Neropalin Blue puts Ridgway's tone word Pale in front of [[dusty-cornflower]], following the same paired-tone method his 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* used across the atlas [1]. Neropalin Blue itself is Ridgway's plate XXII, hue 49, tone b; unlike many of its neighbors it never reached the ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 or Maerz and Paul's 1930 list, so it stayed a Ridgway-only name [1].

Its nearest named neighbor is [[sky-grey]], only 2.5 units off and close enough on screen to read as the same color [1]; [[burn-blue]] sits 3.0 units away and [[cloudy-blue]] 3.3 [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this color in 239 of 23,781 paintings, 1.01 percent, as photographed; narrowing to at least five percent coverage inside a painting leaves 145 [2]. That makes it more common than 65 percent of the named colors in our library [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 1.2 percent of the 1,674 paintings from that century, 1.5 times the archive's overall rate [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light, in 54 percent of its 145 appearances by lightness rank [2].

The earliest match dates to 1450, in a work attributed to Andrea del Castagno, a floor and not a first since the archive's early centuries are thin; that is 462 years before the name's 1912 record, so the match marks a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not a surviving pigment [2]. John Singer Sargent carries it most often, in 4 of his 287 paintings here, though no painter stands out against the museum baseline [2].
